title: Amchem Products, Inc. v. Windsor (1997)
summary: The proposed global asbestos settlement did not satisfy predominance and adequate representation merely because settlement offered common benefits.
notes:
The opinion does not categorically prohibit mass-tort or settlement classes. It requires the class to meet the governing conditions despite the attraction of a comprehensive settlement.

Justice Ginsburg wrote for the Court (6-2, Justice O'Connor not participating); the opinion holds that settlement is relevant to certification because a court need not consider trial-manageability problems, but the other Rule 23 requirements demand undiluted, even heightened, attention in the settlement context, and that predominance is far more demanding than Rule 23(a)(2) commonality.

sections.Parties: Asbestos defendants and proposed class representatives sought approval of a settlement covering present and future claims by a very large population.
sections.Material Facts: The complaint arrived with an agreed settlement. The arrangement provided scheduled payments and a claims process for people with differing exposures, diseases, governing state laws, and future risks. Some were already ill and needed immediate compensation; others had exposure but no current disease and needed preservation of an adequate future fund. Payments lacked inflation protection, and the settlement placed extensive limits on future claims while allowing defendants a later withdrawal mechanism. The proposed class did not provide separate representation for the materially different constituencies.
sections.Procedural History: The district court certified the settlement class and approved the arrangement. The Third Circuit decertified it. The Supreme Court affirmed.
sections.Issue: Could the class be certified based on the benefits and fairness of the settlement despite the differences among the underlying claims and claimants?
sections.Holding: No. The class failed the applicable predominance and representation requirements.
sections.Reasoning: The Court distinguished certification from approval of a fair settlement. Rule 23(e) protects against unfair compromises, while Rule 23(a) and (b) establish when representation is legitimate in the first place. The common desire for compensation could not replace common legal and factual issues in the underlying controversies. Settlement eliminated a need to assess difficulties of trying the case, but other protections deserved undiluted attention because the court would not be able to refine the class through adversarial litigation. The conflict between immediate payments and future protection required structural assurance of representation, rather than confidence that one group of lawyers would balance everyone’s needs.

learning.why: The proposed global asbestos settlement did not satisfy predominance and adequate representation merely because settlement offered common benefits.

topics.cp-settlement-class: A settlement class still had to meet Rule 23(a) and (b), apart from trial-manageability concerns made irrelevant by settlement.
topics.cp-predominance: A common desire for compensation did not make the preexisting claims sufficiently cohesive.
topics.cp-adequate-representation: Presently injured and exposure-only claimants had conflicting allocation interests requiring structural protection.
topics.cp-frcp-23: Amchem is the leading construction of Rule 23(a)(4) and 23(b)(3) in the settlement-class setting.
topics.cp-class-certification: The Court held that settlement does not relax the certification showing except as to trial manageability.

learning.separateOpinions: Justice Breyer, joined by Justice Stevens, agreed that settlement mattered but would have given more weight to its benefits and the district court’s extensive factual findings. He favored further lower-court consideration under the proper standard rather than the majority’s treatment of the record.

mnemonic.rationale: An asbestos settlement class too big to certify
